source.title: Subspace-Aware Sparse Autoencoders for Effective Mechanistic Interpretability

page_placements.theme: Multi-dimensional (circular or manifold) features are fragmented by unit-level analyses

record.tranche_reason: The paper adopts a multidimensional superposition hypothesis as its modeling premise and builds an SAE method around it, but its results concern SAE latent feature splitting, not polysemanticity of individual neurons as specified by the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports original theoretical and empirical results on feature splitting and absorption in sparse autoencoders. These are related to neuron-level polysemanticity but measure a different construct and kind of unit, so the rows are recorded as none rather than assigned to a claim version. Cited findings about standard SAEs were not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The paper assumes the (multi-dimensional) superposition hypothesis and builds a new SAE (SASA) around it. Its results are about SAE latent feature splitting and absorption, plus a method comparison. It reports no rate or degree of polysemanticity in model neurons, whether in vision or language MLPs. So it tests no version of the claim. Its only mention of polysemantic neurons is a cited background statement about Elhage et al. 2022.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is correct. The authors argue that single-direction SAE decoders with coordinate-wise l1 sparsity provably and preferentially split multi-dimensional features. They propose SASA, which consolidates such features into subspace groups. They report that SASA reduces absorption, matches reconstruction quality on about half the token budget, and yields coherent temporal, geographic and sports groups. They make no neuron-level polysemanticity finding.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes and trains sparse autoencoders with vector or subspace decoder units; it does not apply the neuron-level methods or measurements described in the original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: The theoretical split bound depends on intrinsic dimension, co-activation budget, and approximation error. Empirical SAE absorption varies across architecture and model.

fits_no_version.finding: Theory: standard vector-decoder SAEs need exponentially many atoms to cover a multi-dimensional feature. Under the l1 objective, fragmenting the feature lowers the risk below the true-basis solution.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Standard SAEs split multi-dimensional features across many near-collinear latents because their objective favors fragmentation.

fits_no_version.finding: Clusters of standard SAE decoder vectors are larger than the PCA dimension that captures 80% of their variance (median ratio 1.67 for Mistral-7B, 2.18 for GPT-2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Standard SAE dictionaries contain redundant, near-collinear atoms that cover low-dimensional feature subspaces.

fits_no_version.finding: SASA (subspace decoders) shows lower first-letter feature absorption than standard SAEs and the other SAE architectures tested. A theoretical result says SASA consolidates a feature into one block.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Subspace-structured SAEs reduce feature splitting and absorption relative to vector SAEs.

fits_no_version.finding: PCA on raw GPT-2 layer-7 activations shows low-dimensional concept subspaces: dim90 is 14 for temporal concepts and 33 for geography. A mixture of local subspaces explains held-out variance better than global PCA (83.95% vs 74.46%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LLM residual-stream concepts occupy low-dimensional multi-dimensional subspaces.

record.problems: The central theoretical conclusions rely on the paper's single-feature and multidimensional-superposition assumptions. Empirical evaluations cover two model families and use SAE-level benchmarks rather than neuron-level measurements. The decoder-cluster redundancy results use heuristic clustering and are presented in figures without reported uncertainty.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant result rows were omitted. SAE reconstruction and sparsity metrics, group-screening scores used to select groups, and cited results from other work were excluded because they do not directly measure the related SAE feature-splitting or absorption outcomes recorded here.

untested.parts: No measurement of how many MLP neurons in language models are polysemantic, or how this varies by layer. The experiments use residual-stream SAE latents.
Superposition is assumed as a modeling premise (Hypothesis 1). No test links neuron polysemanticity to the number of features exceeding the number of neurons.
Polysemanticity without capacity pressure is not examined.
Architecture is varied for SAEs, not for the base networks. No share of polysemantic neurons is reported.
Canonical polysemantic neurons are not re-examined.
No comparison of neuron polysemanticity measures across activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods.

missing.what: Appendix D: raw GPT-2 activation PCA, with dim90 of 14 (temporal) and 33 (geography), and mixture-of-subspaces held-out variance of 83.95% vs 74.46%. This concerns feature geometry, not neuron polysemanticity, but it is the study's direct evidence for the multi-dimensional superposition premise.

record.verdict_notes: This is an SAE methods paper. 'Polysemantic' appears only in a cited background sentence. The reader's T4/assumes classification is right. All rows are correctly linked to none, and no verdicts apply.

versions.untested_parts: Image-classifier neurons and the InceptionV1 examples are not studied.
The study does not measure polysemanticity of transformer MLP neurons across tokens, contexts, or layers.
It assumes a multidimensional sparse-feature model and analyzes SAE latent splitting, but does not test whether neuron polysemanticity is caused by representing more sparse features than neurons.
It does not test neuron polysemanticity without capacity pressure or attribute it to initialization, regularization, or training noise.
It compares SAE architectures and reports SAE feature-absorption results, not the share of polysemantic neurons or the effects named in this version.
The paper studies SAE feature subspaces and groups, not whether canonical polysemantic neurons detect a shared feature.
It does not compare measurements of neuron polysemanticity across activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods.

rows.subject: Standard SAE decoder (theoretical single-feature slice)
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical lower bound on directions needed to cover a multidimensional feature slice
rows.measure: Minimum number of decoder directions for uniform ε-approximation
rows.note: A theoretical result about SAE feature splitting, not a measurement of neuron polysemanticity.

rows.subject: Standard SAE decoder risk (theoretical single-feature slice)
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical analysis of the ℓ1-regularized decoder-risk landscape
rows.measure: Risk change along a path rotating an extra decoder column toward a diagonal direction
rows.value: The risk is unchanged up to the activation boundary and strictly decreases afterward; the paper gives a lower bound of 2^(−(di+1)) λ²(f(α)−1)²
rows.note: The authors infer that the standard SAE objective favors a fragmented covering solution; this concerns SAE latents rather than neurons.

rows.subject: SASA (theoretical single-feature slice)
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical result on block recovery under the SASA objective
rows.measure: Number of active blocks and recovered feature subspace
rows.value: Every global minimizer activates a single block whose decoder recovers Vi
rows.note: A theoretical consolidation result for SAE feature subspaces, not a neuron-level polysemanticity result.

relation.reason: It takes superposition and polysemantic units as background (Related Work, Hypothesis 1) and tests no polysemantic-neuron version.

tranche.reason: The paper builds a new SAE (SASA) on the multi-dimensional superposition hypothesis. It reports SAE splitting, absorption and reconstruction results, with no measure of neuron polysemanticity.

source_check.notes: R18 and R19 measure redundancy among SAE decoder vectors (feature splitting), not neuron polysemanticity, so they bear on no version. The values are stated in the captions of Figures 6 and 7 in Appendix E, not only plotted.

statements.problem: none; Figures 6 and 7 give median size/PCA-dim ratios of 1.67 (Mistral-7B) and 2.18 (GPT-2) for clusters of size >3, both above the 1.0 line
